data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001 misidentifies the dominant single mechanism governing the *cross-city* variation of the nocturnal UHI. It asserts the gap 'scales with the total thermal mass and impervious surface fraction,' but on a clear, calm night the critical modulator of *how slowly* a city cools — and therefore how large the night-time gap is — is the urban geometry's restriction of radiative cooling: reduced sky view factor (SVF) in dense street canyons suppresses longwave loss to the sky. Thermal mass sets the reservoir, but SVF (building height / street geometry) sets the release bottleneck. Oke's canonical UHI work shows canyon geometry (SVF) is the primary structural control on nocturnal UHI magnitude across cities, not thermal mass per unit area — two cities with similar impervious fractions but different SVFs exhibit materially different nighttime gaps. By attributing the cross-city modulator to thermal mass/impervious fraction alone, the claim conflates the storage reservoir with the release-rate controller and fails to identify the single mechanism the problem asks for.
